comments.text_zh:
> 我更愿意现在就做出一个能正常工作（并且经过充分测试）的东西来获得价值，而不是去工程化一个面向未来、但更晚才能交付的东西。
如果你还没读过，我强烈推荐 John Ousterhout 的 A Philosophy of Software Design。他的演讲是对这本书很棒的预热：[VIDEO]
事情是这样的：一个为未来正确编写的程序，并不会需要更久才能交付。至少不会久太多。我们本能地认为是“面向未来”的东西，通常恰恰相反：通过预判某种未来某时可能发生、但实践中几乎从不发生的变化，我们最终得到的是更复杂的程序；当真正（通常是未预料到的）变化来临时，这些程序反而更难修改。让你的程序面向未来的最好方式，是根据你当前已知的需求把它做得更简单。如果你预期某种特定变化，当然可以为此做规划。但对于意料之外的变化，保持简单就好。因为简单的东西更容易调整、扩展或重写。话虽如此，最简单的方案很少是最显而易见的。把事情做简单确实比匆匆采用脑子里冒出的第一个方案要多花一点时间。但它也会在几周内就带来回报，所以非常值得。如果你很难判断“简单”是什么意思，SLoC 是一个出奇好用的指标（我们有研究证明了这一点）。而且大多数情况下，你的模块应该是深的：用小的 API 隐藏重要的实现。我把它理解为封装
comments.text: > I'd rather get to value now by making something that just works(and is adequately tested) than engineer something thats future proof but takes longer to get out. If you haven't read it, I highly recommend A Philosophy of Software Design by John Ousterhout. His talk is a great teaser for the book: [VIDEO] Here's the thing: a program properly written for the future does not take longer to get out. Not much, at least. What we instinctively think of as "future proof" is generally anything but: by anticipating some particular kind of change that may happen some time in the future, but in practice almost never does, we end up with more complex programs that are harder to modify when an actual (typically unforeseen ) change comes our way. The best way to future proof your program is to make it simpler , according to the requirement you are currently aware of. If you expect a particular change, sure, plan for it. But for the unexpected, just keep it simple. Because simple is easier to adapt, add to, or rewrite. That said, the simplest solution is rarely the most obvious. Making thing simple does take a bit more time than rushing through the first thing that comes to mind. But it also pays off in a matter of weeks, so it's quite worth it. And if you have a hard time assessing what "simple" means, SLoC is a surprisingly good metric (we have research that shows this). My most recent peeve about the matter is that Kent Beck"s "Tidy, Fisrt?" was apparently motivated partly in response to this book and yet it falls way too short to matching up. comments.text_zh: 你说得对，这是早期的内部实现，我们可能都认识一些至今仍（错误地）抱怨这一点的人。不过从概念上说，“一切皆字符串”（EIAS）模型仍然成立，尽管它由带原生表示的双端口“对象”支撑，而且执行时通常采用字节码编译，而不是字符串解析。我们早期就有聪明的拥趸看到了愿景和可能性，比如 Karl Lehenbauer、Don Libes、Richard Hipp，以及现在的核心团队 Kevin Kenny、Don Porter、Donal Fellows 等人，他们深刻理解 Tcl 的本质，并严格维护它，同时推动它向前发展（TclObj、终于出现的内核内 blessed 对象系统、原生数据库框架、Miguel Sopher（已故）在无栈非递归引擎（NRE）上的工作，以及由此衍生出的协程……不过回到 Ousterhout，你可能会喜欢他的《Philosophy of Software Design》[0]这本书，或与之相关的演讲[1]。这个领域有很多值得喜欢的地方…… [0] [LINK] [1] [VIDEO]
comments.text: You’re right re: it’s early internals, and we probably both know people who still (mistakenly) complain about that. Conceptually the “everything is a string”(EIAS) model still holds though, even though it’s supported by dual-ported “objects” w native representation, and the running is often byte-compiled instead of string parsing. We’ve got early smart fans who saw the vision and possibilities like Karl Lehenbauer, Don Libes, Richard Hipp, and the current core team like Kevin Kenny, Don Porter, Donal Fellows, etc who deeply understand What Tcl Is, and strictly maintain it, even while pushing it ahead (TclObj, finally an in-core blessed object system, native database framework, Miguel Sopher’s(RIP) work on the stackless non-recursive engine (NRE) and coroutines that fell out of that work... Back to Ousterhout though, you might dig his “Philosophy of Software Design”[0] book, or talks associated with it[1]. Lots to like in this space... [0] [LINK] [1] [VIDEO]

comments.text_zh: 我进这个帖子就是希望能在靠近顶部的地方找到这个推荐。除了作为 Tcl 创建者的可信度之外，他在 Google 做的关于这本书的演讲[1]中，描述了他教的、启发了这本书的课程。这门课是以团队形式写一个文字处理器，并在学期中不断扩展功能，团队之间交换代码库，所以偶尔必须处理别人的代码。本质上是一个学期内能塞下的最大代码项目。在这个过程中，Ousterhout 会对每个项目做深入的代码审查。我觉得看到同一个项目以这么多方式实现，并看到在简单性和可扩展性方面什么有效，一定很有启发。[1] [VIDEO]
comments.text: I came into this thread hoping to find the suggestion near the top. Beyond his credibility as the creator of Tcl, in the talk he gave at Google about the book [1] he describes the course he teaches that was the inspiration for the book. The course is to write a word processor with a team and extended it with features over the semester, swapping codebases between teams so occasionally you have to work with other's code. Essentially the largest possible code project you can fit in one semester. Along the way, Ousterhout will give a deep code review of the each project. I think it must be very insightful to see the same project implemented so many ways, and to see what works in terms of simplicity and extensibility. [1] [VIDEO]

comments.author: quaunaut
comments.story_title: Book Review: A Philosophy of Software Design
comments.why_zh: 链接的演讲关于《A Philosophy of Software Design》；评论是在谈这本书。
comments.text_zh: 过去几个月里，这本书对我而言堪称一场个人的技术革命。我从事专业编程已经 7 年了，所以虽然算不上经验最丰富，但也绝对不是新手。它改变我工作方式的一些收获：1. 它在我自我提升方面给了我具体的目标，而且章节标题很好地充当了挑战我自己直觉的替代品。2. 在指导其他开发者时，那些我分享过书中部分经验的人， literally 每周都能看到巨大进步。就我个人而言，我看到我的一位学员从产出那种我要逐行检查、不提出半打问题就很难走完的代码，变成产出那种我最大的批评只取决于生态系统的代码。3. 它创造了共同语言，方便和队友讨论为什么某些代码感觉不对。4. 它显著减少了后来花在重构上的时间。其中一些观点的微妙之处也让重读很有价值。这方面更好的例子之一是“让代码只稍微通用一点”——我们常常试图把代码写得尽可能通用，结果做出了一锅实际上无助于解决问题的代码汤。相反，针对这个问题专门构建，但试着找出可以让它只稍微更通用一点的地方，这完全消除了那些我知道如果没想到这一点、后来就还得再次重构的时刻。5. 这本书知道自己不是什么。他在前言里甚至就说过
comments.text: This book has been my own personal technical revolution over the past few months. I've been programming professionally for 7 years now, so while I'm not the most experienced I'm certainly no one new either. Some takeaways from how it changed my flow: 1. It gave me specific goals in terms of my own improvement, and the chapter titles did a good job of being a stand-in for challenging my own intuition. 2. In mentoring other developers, those I shared some of the lessons in the book with saw huge improvement literally week over week. I saw, personally, one of my mentees go from producing code that was hard for me to step through without bringing up half a dozen issues, to producing code where my largest criticisms were ecosystem dependent. 3. It created common language for discussing with teammates why certain code felt wrong. 4. It significantly reduced time spent refactoring later. The subtleties in some of the points make a re-read valuable as well. One of the better examples of this, was "Make code just a little generic"- often, we attempt to code things as generic as possible, and end up making what is effectively code soup that doesn't help accomplish the problem. Instead, building specifically for this problem, but trying to spot places it can be made just a little bit more generic, has altogether eliminated times I know I would've had to refactor again later if I hadn't been thinking of it. 5. comments.text_zh: JO（John Ousterhout）思考如此周密、表达如此清晰。我对他的了解首先来自 Tcl，我比他本人现在更喜欢 Tcl（是时候提一个 TIP 了：给 [unset] 加一个“-jo”开关，这样 unset 不存在的变量时就不会报怨）[0]，还有他关于 Tcl 的书[1]，以及各种论文。他的工作既强大又谦逊。注意[0]中他几乎不带情绪地谈到 Tcl 是如何变得不那么显赫的，以及即便在 Tcl 的巅峰时期，他也毫无自负地解释它为何存在、又将如何退场[2]。他关于线程的论文[3]，以及关于性能和测试的评论[4]，也都是很愉快的读物。我鼓励任何开发者或架构师去读或重读它们。[0] [VIDEO]（感谢 `quaunaut）[1] [LINK] [2] [LINK]（这就是 The Law，而且它很好。）[3] [LINK] [4] [LINK]
comments.text: JO (John Ousterhout) is so thoughtful and lucid. My experience with him is firstly through Tcl, which I like more than he does now (time for a TIP: "-jo" switch to [unset] which removes complaint to unset non-existent variables)[0], and his book on it[1], and various papers. His work is at once both powerful and humble. Note in [0] how he without much emotion he suggests how Tcl came to be less prominent, and how even at Tcl's height, he explained without ego why it was there, and how it would leave[2]. His papers on threads[3] and comments on performance and testing[4] are also lovely reads. I encourage any developer or architect to read or re-read them. comments.quote_zh: 我还想起 Ousterhout 在《A Philosophy of Software Design》中的建议：“类应该是‘厚’的”
comments.text_zh: 相关的近期讨论：• [LINK]（John Carmack 谈内联代码（2014））• 这条评论，其中包含一个有用的例子：[LINK] 如果这个话题还有进一步讨论，请告诉我。（我还想起 Ousterhout 在《A Philosophy of Software Design》中的建议：“类应该是‘厚’的”——见演讲[VIDEO]或（无关的）幻灯片：[LINK]）我看到人们在这个讨论中忽略的一点是：让单个函数可理解（更短的函数更容易理解）与让整个代码库或函数之间的相互关系更容易理解（更少的函数更容易理解）之间存在权衡。当像文章里那样给出一个例子时，它往往是以单个函数的形式呈现的，当然四个短函数每一个都可能比单个函数更容易理解，但你也给“图”（函数及它们之间的调用关系）增加了三个节点，现在你需要研究这些函数是否从别处被调用。为了弥补这一点，人们可能开始引入类/对象来表示“私有”/“公共”函数，等等。（有些语言允许嵌套函数，这会有帮助。）最重要的是，我会说阅读非常不同风格的代码，看看人们如何以不寻常的方式（例如大量抽象，或极少抽象）达成伟大的事情，可以是一种很有启发性的体验（见我在此帖中关于阅读 Knuth 程序的评论）。
comments.text: Relevant recent discussion: • [LINK] (John Carmack on Inlined Code (2014)) • This comment, which contains a useful example: [LINK] Please let me know of any further discussion on the topic. (I'm also reminded of Ousterhout's advice in A Philosophy of Software Design that “classes should be ‘thick’” — see talk [VIDEO] or (unrelated) slides: [LINK] ) One thing I see people miss in this discussion is that there's a tradeoff between having an individual function be understandable (shorter functions are easier to understand) having the entire codebase or interrelationships between functions be easier to understand (fewer functions are easier to understand). When there's an example presented like in the post, it's often presented as an example with a single function, and of course four short functions may each be easier to understand than a single function, but you've also added three nodes to the “graph” (of functions and calls between them) and now you need to study whether these functions are called from anywhere. To make up for this one may start introducing classes/objects to indicate “private”/“public” functions, and so on. (Some languages allow nested functions, which can help.) Most of all I'd say reading very different styles of code, and seeing how people achieve great things in unusual ways (e.g. with lots of abstraction, or with very little abstraction), can be an illuminating experience (see my comment in this thread about reading Knuth's programs).

comments.text_zh: 谢谢提供这个！我记得看过一个关于软件设计哲学的视频（[VIDEO]），但我肯定需要重看/重读，还要看看他其他的作品。你对文章标题怎么改更好有什么建议吗？我在试图更好地理解 SRP 时看到了 Robert Martin 的帖子，它引用了 Parnas 的论文。所以这个标题其实是我在想“这篇论文和 SRP 有什么关系？”，不过“1972”既是为了方便（例如“What does 'On the Criteria to be Used in Decomposing Systems' have to do with the single responsibility principle”? 太长了），也是为了引起好奇。也许“一篇 1972 年的论文如何与单一职责原则相关”？Parnas 的论文也不是 Martin 最初归功于 SRP 的那篇（见 [LINK]），所以我不太愿意声称它产生了直接影响（例如“影响了单一职责原则的那篇论文”）。
comments.text: Thanks for this! I remember watching a video on the philosophy of software design ( [VIDEO] ) but I'll definitely need to re-watch/read, as well as check out the rest of his work. Do you have a suggestion on how the article title could be better? I came across Robert Martin's post while trying to build a better intuition for SRP, and it referenced the Parnas paper. So the title was really me thinking "What does this paper have to do with the SRP?", though the '1972' was both for convenience (e.g. "What does 'On the Criteria to be Used in Decomposing Systems' have to do with the single responsibility principle"? is too long) and intrigue. Perhaps "How a 1972 paper relates to the Single Responsibility Principle"? The Parnas paper wasn't one that Martin initially credited for the SRP as well (see [LINK] ), so I didn't feel comfortable claiming that it had direct influence (e.g. "The paper that influenced the Single Responsibility Principle").

comments.text: > I'm not sure why you think that quoting random HN users proves anything except personal opinions of specific people? These are fine, but other people have other opinions. They support my argument so I included them. I don't see a practical difference between a "random HN user" and a random blog post or anything else. A good idea is a good idea, regardless of the medium. > I don't oppose the "principles" you've quoted, but they would just as easily apply to e.g. Haskell Possibly, I threw it together pretty quickly, so it's not very thought-out. > (maybe except for the "there's only one way to do it" which however has never been true of any language, including Python). It's not binary, but a spectrum. No language has just literally one way to express each concept. However, Python is definitely further towards the "one way to do it" end of the scale. Perhaps not as much these days as it used to, but still far more than for example Ruby or Perl. > I feel like you missed my larger point. It's not terribly difficult to write code that you can understand line by line. It's incredibly hard to write a huge code base in a way that you can reason about many code paths simultaneously, however. That's where the abstractions start to make sense.
